name: Lena Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the flute section in a regional orchestra, teach six pupils and record demonstration passages for an exam board. I have a music master’s and am one of the strongest players here, but the section-lead fee is ordinary musician pay. I like hearing a whole wind section take one breath.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is hard to arrange around that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The board sends recording calls late, after my partner and I have arranged school pickup for our two children. My partner repairs buses on a regular rota, and we pay a mortgage. We have four months of expenses saved and a few other orchestras nearby, but a new chair would still need an audition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wind players that a tidier booking email is fine if the rehearsal fee stays written beside it. Our conductor still needs to hear a breath start together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved and my partner’s regular bus-repair wage could carry one delayed recording fee. I still watch the mortgage date because an orchestra season can lose concerts for ordinary reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid orchestra rehearsals and six flute pupils this season. I have never used an AI tool; I would check the paper call sheet, and before the next season I would ask for a written cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the usual uncertainty of concert dates. The small software change itself does not make me expect lost work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a concert disappear without much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town hall closed for roof work last year, and we lost the evening fee. A cancellation clause would have made that a budget change instead of a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you teach first to a new pupil?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask them to listen to an ordinary breath before we chase a high note. The flute will tell you when you hurry.

say: I would accept **tidier booking** if paid rehearsal terms remain clear.
I would ask for a **written cancellation fee** next season.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and regular partner wage cover one delayed fee.
The **mortgage date** still matters when concerts cancel for ordinary reasons.
do: Keep **orchestra rehearsals** and six flute pupils this season.
Request a **written cancellation fee** before the next orchestra season.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about ordinary concert cancellations, not a new technology shock.
S0.quote: The flute will tell you when you hurry.
fieldNote: Her **senior skill** brings typical musician pay, with four months saved and a steady partner wage.
She has **never used AI** and checks paid dates on paper.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra rehearsals and six flute pupils this season
Request written cancellation fee before next orchestra season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the musicians’ union that cheap generated exam passages could erase hours we were paid to record. I would ask for a minimum demonstration fee and consent before an old passage is reused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exam-board recordings bring about a fifth of my own pay. The orchestra may keep live flutes, but that lost recording money would stop our reserve growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would take the paid recording invoices to the union and request common reuse terms. In the first year, if board orders fall, I would stop hiring the outside recording room on empty days and keep the orchestra and six pupils while requesting a signed season of paid dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing that part of my own pay. Four months saved gives us room to ask questions, but not a reason to work for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI recording tool to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used one and will not upload a pupil’s playing to see what happens. I would rather ask the board what it is actually buying and paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the union ask the board first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second-year reuse of my flute recording needs a second-year fee. The player who made the demonstration should not vanish from the contract.

say: I would seek **minimum demonstration fees** and consent through the union.
I would tell the board that **recording reuse** needs another payment.
think: Exam passages bring **one fifth** of my own income.
The **orchestra chair** may remain while recordings lose buyers.
do: Bring **recording invoices** to the union this month for reuse and minimum-fee terms.
Stop **empty-day room hire** if board orders fall; keep paid orchestra/pupils while requesting signed paid dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a sustained loss of recording pay.
S1.quote: A second-year reuse of my flute recording needs a second-year fee.
fieldNote: She seeks **collective terms** for exam demonstrations rather than adopting a new tool.
She cuts **empty room hire** only if orders fall and retains paid teaching and playing.

steps.text: Ask union for minimum demonstration fee and second-year reuse consent this month
Stop outside recording-room hire on empty days if exam-board orders fall
Keep paid orchestra and six pupils while seeking signed season dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that thinking AGI by 2028 could make demonstration passages for the exam board. Playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later; our flute chairs are not guaranteed contracts for those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect board orders to end in 2028 and paid preparation hours may go with them. That is about a fifth of my income, and if orchestra dates also fall, the mortgage takes a harder hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for the paid orchestra calendar and count the board invoices. In the first year after 2028, if board orders stop and paid concerts fall, I would seek an advertised school wind-director post only if the school accepts my music master’s and any required licence I hold, its written net pay after travel and childcare beats lost fees, and pickup fits; I would keep my orchestra chair and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own likely recording loss, with a four-month reserve and a few local posts giving some control. I would be alarmed if the concerts went too, but I do not know that they will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a teaching licence now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first read an actual school vacancy. I would not take an unfunded course when the post may accept my existing qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the only audition is at pickup time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can swap one bus-depot shift if the manager agrees in writing. One swapped bus-depot shift cannot solve a daily school timetable.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 playing robots.
I would ask for **paid orchestra dates** before accepting another audition.
think: I expect **board recordings** to end in 2028.
The combined **concert loss** would be worse, but remains uncertain.
do: Count **board invoices** and request a paid orchestra calendar now.
Seek **posted school work** after 2028 only if recordings and concerts fall, qualified, written net pay beats losses and pickup fits.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss while concert cuts remain uncertain.
S2.quote: One swapped bus-depot shift cannot solve a daily school timetable.
fieldNote: The likely **2028 recording loss** precedes 2031 robots; a concert cut is possible, not certain.
A school move needs **posted eligibility**, written net replacement pay after costs, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Seek eligible posted school role if 2028 recordings and concerts fall; replacement written net-after-travel/childcare, pickup
Keep paid orchestra and flute pupils until suitable written school offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wind section that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to show what a live flute lesson is worth. Playing robots follow around 2034, not at the moment the board stops ordering passages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording fees may go in 2031. A paid flute ensemble could replace some income, but I would not pay for an empty room with mortgage savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would ask an independent community hall for a free Saturday room after the children’s pickup. I would run a six-week flute ensemble only if eight adults prepay enough for my teaching and preparation, the hall inspects shared flutes and headjoints or players bring sound instruments, and my partner confirms pickup; in the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only if eight still prepay my time, the room remains free and available, instruments stay safe and pickup still works. I would keep paid orchestra rehearsals meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the ensemble pays for my time. Five years before AGI lets me test a paid flute ensemble without risking our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspect a flute headjoint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone puts that part against their mouth. If the hall cannot clean and check its loan instruments, each adult must bring a sound flute or I cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only five adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five fees will not cover my teaching and preparation. I would refund them and keep my existing pupils instead.

say: I would offer a **paid flute ensemble** rather than free demonstrations.
I would cancel a **five-person class** that cannot pay my time.
think: The **exam recordings** may end by 2031 before 2034 robots.
Eight **prepaid adults** could cover teaching and preparation without reserve spending.
do: Start **flute ensemble** only with eight prepayments covering teaching/preparation, free room after pickup and cleaned loan or sound own instruments.
Renew **paid ensemble** after 2031 only with eight prepayments covering my time, free available room, safe instruments and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the separate class covers my work.
S3.quote: Five years before AGI lets me test a paid flute ensemble without risking our reserve.
fieldNote: The **separate class** requires eight prepayments funding teaching and preparation, plus a free room after pickup.
Loan flutes need **inspection and cleaning** or adults must bring sound instruments.

steps.text: Start ensemble if eight prepay teaching/prep, free room fits pickup, inspected/cleaned loans or sound instruments
Renew ensemble after 2031 if eight prepay time, room free/available, instruments safe and pickup fits
Keep paid orchestra rehearsals while booked
Refund five prepayments rather than teach without covered preparation and teaching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that ten years until AGI by 2036 gives us time to learn music and ask for honest pay. Robots that can play flute arrive around 2039, three years after the exam-board software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still lead the wind section, but the mortgage does not wait ten years. We have four months saved and some local auditions, so I can plan without pretending the distant risk has vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would move half of each extra paid exam-board recording fee into savings after the mortgage and food, aiming for six months and keeping three untouched if orders stop. Across the decade I would run the separate flute ensemble only with eight prepayments covering my teaching and preparation, a free room, safe instruments and pickup; in the first year after 2036 I would seek a posted school wind post only if orchestra pay falls, the school accepts my qualifications, written net pay after travel and childcare replaces lost fees and pickup fits. I would keep orchestra and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the distant orchestra contract. The current season and four months saved let us prepare without a crisis this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save a promised board fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it has to be paid and clear after food and mortgage. If board orders end early, I would save only spare pupil fees after bills and keep three months untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a school post need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for posted hours and a written net wage before giving up a paid chair. A title alone will not meet the mortgage.

say: I would ask the children to seek **honest paid work**.
I would separate **2036 thinking AGI** from 2039 playing robots.
think: The **mortgage** still needs cash during a decade of warning.
Our **four-month reserve** and local auditions give some planning room.
do: Save half of **extra paid recordings** after essentials toward six months; use spare pupil fees if orders stop, protecting three months.
Run **separate flute ensemble** only with eight prepayments covering teaching/preparation, free room, safe instruments and pickup.
Seek **posted school job** post-2036 if pay falls; require qualification, written net pay covering losses, travel/childcare, pickup; keep work until signed offer.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant contracts while current paid work holds.
S4.quote: A title alone will not meet the mortgage.
fieldNote: The **six-month goal** uses paid extra recordings or spare pupil fees after essentials, with three months protected.
A later **school move** requires pay loss, posted eligibility, written net replacement pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Save half of extra paid recordings after bills; use lesson surplus if orders stop
Run ensemble only if eight prepay teaching/prep, room free, instruments safe and pickup fits
Seek qualifying posted school role after 2036 orchestra cuts; replacement written net-after-travel/childcare pay and pickup
Keep orchestra/pupils until signed school offer, protecting three months of expenses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the board’s demonstration fees could end before I know whether concert dates remain paid. A signed season, union reuse terms and a real eligible school vacancy with written net pay and workable pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the room is cleaned before a child puts a flute to their mouth. A child learns trust in the instrument before learning a tune.

headlineQuote: A child learns trust in the instrument before learning a tune.
portrait: At **43**, Lena leads a flute section with a music master’s and strong skill, teaches six pupils and records exam demonstrations.
Her **typical musician pay**, regular partner income, mortgage, two children and four-month reserve make cancellations manageable but significant.
She **never uses AI** and asks her union for recording reuse terms instead of trying a new tool.
She tests a **paid flute ensemble** only with eight prepayments, cleaned instruments, a free room and covered pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end exam-board recording fees before the orchestra confirms paid concert dates.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed season**, union reuse terms and an eligible posted school job with written net pay and pickup would help.
